sections.heading: C — Sharing the road part one: vulnerable road users, crosswalk stops, school zones, white canes, bicycles and bike boxes, motorcycles and large vehicles
sections.markdown:
## C — Sharing the road part one: vulnerable road users, crosswalk stops, school zones, white canes, bicycles and bike boxes, motorcycles and large vehicles
Knowledge domain: who counts as a vulnerable road user, when you must stop and stay stopped for pedestrians, how school speed zones work, and how to share the road with bicyclists, motorcyclists and large vehicles; buses, pilot vehicles, oversize loads, processions and stopped vehicles continue in part C2.

FACT_ID: sec06-F01 | anchor: A01
Vulnerable road users include pedestrians, bicyclists, motorcyclists, highway workers and anyone using a skateboard, scooter or similar device in a public way, a crosswalk or on a highway shoulder. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F02 | anchor: A01
These road users are called vulnerable because they can be hard to see and often have no protection from injury in a crash. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F03 | anchor: A01
In the manual the word pedestrian covers people walking and people rolling on skateboards, scooters, wheelchairs and similar devices. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F04 | anchor: A01
You must stop for a pedestrian crossing the road at any crosswalk, whether it is marked or unmarked. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F05 | anchor: A01
A pedestrian is legally crossing as soon as any part of the person, or something they use such as a cane, wheelchair or bicycle, moves onto the road. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F06 | anchor: A01
Stop and stay stopped for a crosswalk pedestrian who is in your lane, in the lane beside yours (a bike lane counts), or in the lane you are turning into. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F07 | anchor: A02
When turning at an intersection with a traffic signal, the pedestrian must be at least 6 feet from the lane you are turning into before you start the turn. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F08 | anchor: A02
When turning at an intersection without a traffic signal, the pedestrian must have cleared the lane you are turning into and the next lane too before you start the turn. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F09 | anchor: A02
It is illegal to pass a vehicle that is stopped at a crosswalk, since its driver may be waiting for someone to cross. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F10 | anchor: A02
You do not have to stop for a pedestrian who is in a crosswalk on the far side of a safety island. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F11 | anchor: A02
Every intersection has a crosswalk even with no painted lines; to find an unmarked one, picture the corner sidewalk or shoulder carried across the road. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F12 | anchor: A02
An unmarked crosswalk is at least 6 feet wide, and it exists even where there is no sidewalk or shoulder. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F13 | anchor: A02
A mid-block crosswalk may have a flashing yellow light that warns a pedestrian is crossing or about to cross. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F14 | anchor: A02
Never stop with any part of your vehicle over the crosswalk, because a blocked crosswalk forces pedestrians around your car into danger. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F15 | anchor: A02
When you cross a sidewalk to enter or leave a parking lot, alley or driveway, stop before the sidewalk and yield to pedestrians and bicyclists. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-F16 | anchor: A03
A school zone is a stretch of road beside a school or a school crosswalk that signs mark as a school zone. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F17 | anchor: A03
A yellow five-sided sign marks where a school zone begins and warns of school crossings, so look for children and be ready to stop. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F18 | anchor: A03
A school speed zone carries a reduced limit of 20 mph, beginning at the SCHOOL SPEED LIMIT 20 sign and ending at the END SCHOOL ZONE sign or another posted speed sign. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F19 | anchor: A03
When the yellow light on a school speed sign is flashing, children are arriving at or leaving school and the reduced limit applies. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F20 | anchor: A03
A school-hours speed sign applies from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. on days school is in session, and if you are unsure whether it is a school day, slow to 20 mph. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F21 | anchor: A03
A school speed sign for when children are present applies on any day and at any hour that children are present. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F22 | anchor: A03
Children are present when they are waiting at a crosswalk, are in or walking through a crosswalk, or a traffic patrol member is there to help them cross. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F23 | anchor: A03
Yield to a pedestrian with limited vision, or one who is blind or deaf and blind using a white cane or guide dog: stop if the person is crossing or about to, and stay stopped until they have crossed the whole road, even on a green light. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F24 | anchor: A03
In neighborhoods and near parks, keep away from parked cars that hide your view and take great care backing out of a driveway, since children may be playing behind your vehicle. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-F25 | anchor: A04
Stop and yield when children step into a crosswalk or a school crossing guard signals you, and stay stopped until the children are out of the crosswalk. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec06-F26 | anchor: A04
Bicyclists are harder to see than other vehicles and can be hidden in your blind spot. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec06-F27 | anchor: A04
Potholes, glass, litter, storm grates, railroad tracks and car doors opening can make a bicyclist slow or swerve into your path, so leave riders plenty of room. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec06-F28 | anchor: A04
Never drive or park in a bike lane; crossing one is allowed to turn or to get into or out of an alley, driveway or private road. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec06-F29 | anchor: A04
Before turning across a bike lane or sidewalk you must yield to bicyclists using it, and at intersections you yield to bicyclists just as you would to other vehicles. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec06-F30 | anchor: A04
At speeds above 35 mph, you may pass a bicyclist in your lane only if you leave enough distance that you would not hit the rider if they fell. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec06-F31 | anchor: A05
Ordinary passing rules apply to bicyclists too, and if you cannot pass safely you slow down and stay behind the rider until you can. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec06-F32 | anchor: A05
Motorized wheelchairs, scooters and personal assistive mobility devices may use bike lanes and paths, and you yield to their operators as you would to a bicyclist. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec06-F33 | anchor: A05
A bike box is usually a green painted box marked with a white bicycle symbol; at a signal you stop behind it, never inside it, and bicyclists move into the box ahead of you. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec06-F34 | anchor: A05
Where there is a bike box, right turns on a red light are not allowed, and when turning right on green you signal and yield to bicyclists on your right. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec06-F35 | anchor: A05
A sharrow, two chevrons painted above a bicycle symbol, shows a shared lane where bicyclists may be riding in the road. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec06-F36 | anchor: A06
Motorcycles and mopeds are harder to see than other vehicles, and it is hard to judge how far away a rider is or how fast they are going. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec06-F37 | anchor: A06
You must yield to an oncoming motorcyclist just as you would to any vehicle, and the safest choice is to wait until the rider passes before you turn. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec06-F38 | anchor: A06
Leave more following distance behind a motorcycle than you would behind a car. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec06-F39 | anchor: A06
Some motorcycle turn signals do not cancel by themselves, so before turning in front of an oncoming rider with a signal on, make sure the rider is really slowing to turn. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec06-F40 | anchor: A06
Sharing a lane with a motorcycle or moped is against the law, and when you pass one you must leave the rider a full lane. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec06-F41 | anchor: A06
Strong wind and surfaces such as gravel, debris, pavement seams, grooved pavement and manhole covers can make riders change speed or direction, so increase your following distance. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec06-F42 | anchor: A07
Large vehicles such as recreational vehicles, trucks, buses and vehicles towing trailers accelerate slowly, need more room, and need about three times the stopping distance of a smaller vehicle at the same speed. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec06-F43 | anchor: A07
Large vehicles have bigger blind spots on both sides, and if you cannot see the driver in the large vehicle's side mirror, that driver cannot see you. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec06-F44 | anchor: A07
A large vehicle has a deep blind spot right behind it, and you should not stop too close behind one because it may roll back slightly when it starts. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec06-F45 | anchor: A07
Passing a large vehicle takes longer, so finish quickly, do not ride alongside it, and wait until its entire front appears in your rearview mirror before moving back in. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec06-F46 | anchor: A07
On a wet road, spray from a large vehicle can badly reduce your vision, so stay as far from it as you can while keeping to your lane. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec06-F47 | anchor: A07
Never cut in between a turning large vehicle and the curb or shoulder, because it may swing wide and use more than one lane, and do not crowd the intersection while it turns. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0061]

Misconceptions: an unmarked crosswalk is still a crosswalk at every intersection; a pedestrian on the far side of a safety island does not require a stop, but one in the lane beside yours does; a children-present school sign applies at any hour and on any day, not only during school hours; a green light does not end the duty to wait for a white-cane or guide-dog pedestrian; the bicycle fall-distance passing rule is tied to speeds above a set limit, not to every pass; sharing a lane with a motorcycle is illegal, not a courtesy.
Mnemonics: any part on the road means crossing; signal means wait for a clear six-foot gap, no signal means two lanes clear; if you cannot see the mirror, the trucker cannot see you; full lane for every motorcycle.
Glossary: vulnerable road user means a pedestrian, bicyclist, motorcyclist, highway worker or rolling-device user; unmarked crosswalk means the crossing formed by extending the corner sidewalk or shoulder; bike box means a green painted stop area for bicyclists ahead of cars at a signal; sharrow means a shared-lane marking of chevrons over a bicycle; blind spot means an area the driver cannot see even with mirrors.
Dynamic facts: school speed zones depend on time and presence, since the school-hours sign applies only during set hours on school days and the children-present sign applies only while children are present.

corpus_stability.reason: The Oregon Driver Manual is a two-year edition (the front cover names a two-year span and the back cover carries a single form revision code); fees and office details are sent to the DMV website rather than printed, and nothing in the selected pages suggests more than one rewrite per year.
